speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: asked the Minister for Law (a) whether he can provide an update on the implementation of the Family Justice Committee's reforms; (b) whether there has been an assessment of the outcomes of the cases at the Family Justice Courts after the introduction of the various reforms; (c) whether further enhancements can be made to the Court processes to encourage families to heal and reconcile; and (d) how can the family law practitioners be part of this change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our family justice system aims to resolve family disputes through mediation as far as possible and with litigation only as the last resort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Many cases that go through the family justice system are divorce proceedings and ancillary issues, such as the division of matrimonial assets and issues relating to the custody, care and control of the children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Court process in dealing with these issues should be affordable and should not make it more painful for the families involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In particular, we should see to the interests of the children and protect them during the proceedings to the extent possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With these aims in mind, the Committee for Family Justice was convened in 2013, which made recommendations to introduce less adversarial and more child-centric approaches in family proceedings and to also improve community support outside of the Court system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The work of the Committee led to the enactment of the Family Justice Act and the establishment of the Family Justice Courts on 1 October 2014.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Pursuant to the Committee's recommendations, the following reforms were implemented in the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This was adopted and places the judge in the centre of the Court process and allows the judge to guide and direct the proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This reduces acrimony between parties and is an improvement over the previous purely adversarial approach towards resolving family disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, case management policies and processes have been enhanced in the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The docketing system ensures that a single judge manages the case early in the proceedings to its conclusion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This helps to ensure that the judicial officer adjudicating the dispute is familiar with, and sensitive to, the issues and parties involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The simplified uncontested divorce track was also implemented to allow parties to apply for the case to be scheduled for an uncontested hearing if there has been agreement on both sides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Cases under the simplified uncontested divorce track are resolved faster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Previously, the median time taken for such cases to obtain Interim Judgment was 53 days.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This was shortened to about 20 days under the simplified uncontested divorce track.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, child representatives are now appointed by the Court if it is in the best interests of the child to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This usually occurs in high conflict matters where parties cannot agree on the care arrangements of the child.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are currently 26 trained child representatives, and there have since been 40 cases where child representatives were appointed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These child representatives represent the voice of the child in family disputes and present an objective assessment of the care arrangements which would be in the best interests of the child.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Fourth, aside from the Court-based initiatives, the Committee also recognised that families should be provided with better assistance and support to resolve their disputes out-of-Court, wherever possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In this regard, the Committee proposed the establishment of Divorce Support Specialist Agencies to provide specialised services and programmes for divorcing and divorced families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) has since established four Divorce Support Specialist Agencies to provide the support and care to such families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Family Justice Courts have been established for three years now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We intend to work with the Family Justice Courts to conduct a joint survey of Court users to better understand the Court users' experience of the reforms in the family justice system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Despite these improvements, certain cases still require an extended time to resolve and with acute acrimony between the parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Family lawyers play an important and integral role in these reforms, including how they advise and counsel clients, the manner in which they conduct the cases in Court and their knowledge and familiarity with the social support systems that have been set up to assist families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This was recognised by the Committee for Family Justice which proposed a new Family Law Practitioner accreditation scheme for lawyers who have undergone specialist training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Work is underway to design a specialist family law and multidiscipline training for family lawyers and I look forward to the implementation of this recommendation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will continue to partner and support our family lawyers to facilitate the effective practice of family law today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a very pertinent point – attendance in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court is an important institution and people must understand that Court hearings are to be respected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Courts and the justice that they dispense underpin our entire societal system, not least in family law cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I would urge anybody who receives a Court summons, whether it be family law or anything else, to give it due attention, due weight and to respect the Court as an institution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where the document calls for attendance before the Court, it is very important that that person must turn up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are sometimes when a person is unable to turn up for various reasons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this scenario, there are a few options.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, if the person is represented, usually a lawyer will take care of that, and the lawyer can appear on your behalf and you do not have to be there, unless there are certain very specific things, such as your having to give evidence because the trial is ongoing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In that case, clearly, the lawyer cannot be giving evidence on your behalf.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if for some reason you are ill, unwell, have some other really pressing commitment which the Court agrees takes precedence, you can ask the Court for adjournment and the lawyer will do that for you.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But there are many parties who are not represented.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If not, they can also approach their Member of Parliament at the Meet-the-People sessions to write to MinLaw, which will then forward the letter to the Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the end of the day, the important thing to remember is that Court proceedings are important and people must appear.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those who meet the means test, there is also legal aid representation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They can also go to the Law Society Pro Bono Office and there are the legal clinics which are conducted by the Community Development Councils.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is also the Community Justice Centre at the State Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those who need legal assistance, I would urge them to seek out these options.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Family law proceedings are not like other proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not like commercial litigation, for example, where what is at stake is really money, by and large.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, even if it is a question of an extra hundred thousand dollars, an extra million dollars, it is still money.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But in family proceedings, it is a lot to do with emotions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Very often, it has to do with the impact on the child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In commercial proceedings, how do you measure win and lose?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You measure by how much money you get, the amount of damages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But how do you measure win and lose in litigation proceedings for family cases?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You often find that for the parties, winning actually means hurting the other side, taking the other side's assets as much as you can, or preventing the other side from having access to the child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is how winning and losing are very often measured in family cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The measure for winning and losing in family cases should really be how are you able to disentangle your lives after having been together for a long time, with the least pain possible, and in a way that allows you to move on, emotionally as well as in terms of other arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other measure should be how do you do it in a way that least adversely impacts a child?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Once these become your measures, you can begin to see how the training and the skillsets for the lawyers have to be very different.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because in commercial litigation, it is about how you can score the legal points and how you can get the extra money.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But here, as a lawyer, you have to counsel your client.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If your client is determined to get at the other side by withholding access to the child, that is not in the child's best interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the lawyer has to be trained to deal with that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When I was in practice, I had a case where whenever the children had telephone access to the father, the mother would not allow the children to take the call from the telephone in the living room.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She would banish them to the balcony in the kitchen where all the washing and the drying and the clothes were.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In their minds, every time they take a call from their father, they have to go out into the balcony and sit out there, like it is not a normal family activity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The children would feel a bit like it was punishment whenever they took a call from their father.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are things where the lawyer should be able to advise the client and, where necessary, advise them where to go for counselling.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If your client is somebody who has been accused of domestic violence, does that person have something wrong with him or her where he or she feels a need to take out his or her anger and frustration on the spouse?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Increasingly, these are not just purely domestic issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are more and more marriages which are cross-border these days, so you will then have to deal with issues that will require knowledge of the international conventions that deal with children and cross-border marriages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is something we are studying and looking to see how we can make more seamless.
